Warm Up: Spring-Mass System — Sketching a Solution Curve

Sketch an approximate solution to the system of first-order differential equations with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v \\[8pt] \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -0.18x \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = 3,\quad v(0) = 0\]
Diagram description: A vector field is shown in the \(xv\)-plane (displacement \(x\) on the horizontal axis, velocity \(v\) on the vertical axis), both axes ranging from \(-5\) to \(5\). The blue arrows form a counterclockwise rotation pattern consistent with closed elliptical orbits around the origin. Starting from \((3,\, 0)\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, the solution traces a closed ellipse as the spring oscillates. An interactive drawing interface (Clear All, Draw: Freehand Draw, Eraser) is provided for students to sketch the solution.

Page 4

Recall: Approaches to Systems of Equations

Given systems of equations, we have studied several approaches:

  1. Quantitative Situation — modeling a real-world scenario as a system
  2. Visualizations — vector fields and solution curves
  3. Numerical Methods — Euler’s method
  4. Analytic Solutions
        → Parametric Curves ← Now

Page 5

Parametric Curves — Definition

Definition: A parametric curve is a vector-valued function

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\]

where both \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) are functions of the parameter \(t\). It describes the path a particle takes on the plane. Its position at time parameter \(t\) is given by \(\vec{r}(t)\).

Page 6

Parametric Curves — First Examples

① Graphs

If \(f(t)\) is a continuous function, then

\[\vec{F}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t \\ f(t) \end{bmatrix}\]

is precisely the graph of \(f(t)\).

Diagram description: A sketch shows a horizontal axis labeled \(t\) and a vertical axis. A curve representing \(f(t)\) rises and then levels off. A point on the curve is annotated with the position vector \(\begin{bmatrix} t \\ f(t) \end{bmatrix}\), showing that the parametric curve traces exactly the graph of \(f\).

Page 7

Parametric Curves — Conics

② Conics — Circles and Ellipses

Circles and ellipses are not graphs of functions (they fail the vertical line test). However, they can be described as parametric curves:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} a\cos t \\ b\sin t \end{bmatrix} = \langle a\cos t,\; b\sin t \rangle\]

The left form is column notation and the right is row notation (angle bracket form). When \(a = b\) this gives a circle; when \(a \neq b\) it gives an ellipse.

Diagram description: A sketch shows an ellipse centered at the origin with its major axis along the horizontal direction, illustrating the shape traced by \(\vec{r}(t) = \langle a\cos t, b\sin t \rangle\).

Page 8

Parametric Curves — Exercise: Plot from Component Functions

Given the two functions \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), plot the parametric curve in the \(xy\)-plane.

Diagram description: Two component graphs are shown side by side. The left graph shows \(x = f(t)\): starting at 0, rising linearly to 1 between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\), remaining at 1 between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 2\), then falling linearly back to 0 between \(t = 2\) and \(t = 3\), staying at 0 to \(t = 4\) (a trapezoid shape). The right graph shows \(y = g(t)\): starting at 0, staying at 0 between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\), rising linearly to 1 between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 2\), staying at 1 between \(t = 2\) and \(t = 3\), then falling to 0 at \(t = 4\) (a trapezoid offset by one unit in \(t\)).

Annotated key points on the resulting \(xy\)-curve are:

  • \(t = 0\): position \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) — at the origin
  • \(t = 1\): position \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) — on positive \(x\)-axis
  • \(t = 2\): position \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) — upper right
  • \(t = 3\): position \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) — upper left
Resulting \(xy\)-curve description: A handwritten sketch below the graphs shows the parametric curve in the \(xy\)-plane. The curve travels from the origin rightward to \((1,0)\), then up to \((1,1)\), then left to \((0,1)\), tracing three sides of a square. Red dots mark the key positions at each integer value of \(t\), and green arrows show the direction of travel.

Parametric Curves — Exercise: Triangular Path

Given the two functions \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), plot the parametric curve in the \(xy\)-plane.

Diagram description: Two component graphs are shown side by side, both with axes ranging from \(-1\) to \(1\) vertically and \(0\) to \(4\) horizontally. The left graph shows \(x = f(t)\): starting at 0, rising linearly to \(1\) at \(t = 1\), falling linearly to \(-1\) at \(t = 3\), then rising again (a triangle wave). A red dot marks the starting point at \((0, 0)\). The right graph shows \(y = g(t)\): starting at \(-1\) at \(t = 0\), rising linearly to \(1\) at \(t = 2\), then falling linearly back to \(-1\) at \(t = 4\) (a triangle wave offset by one unit relative to \(f\)).
Resulting \(xy\)-curve description: The handwritten \(xy\)-sketch shows the parametric curve traces a diamond (rhombus) shape in the plane. Starting at \((0,\,-1)\), the particle travels to \((1,\,0)\), then to \((0,\,1)\), then to \((-1,\,0)\), and back toward \((0,\,-1)\). Red dots mark the four vertices and the green arrows show the direction of travel as \(t\) increases, going counterclockwise around the diamond.

Page 10

Parametric Curves — Tangent Vector

Theorem: If \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) where \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) are differentiable, then \(\vec{r}(t)\) is a smooth (or differentiable) curve and its tangent vector is

\[\vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x'(t) \\ y'(t) \end{bmatrix}\]

(prime here means derivative with respect to the parameter \(t\)).

Diagram description: A GeoGebra interactive applet is shown. The parametric curve is defined by \(f_x(t) = 2\sin(C_1 t)\cos(t)\) and \(f_y(t) = 2\sin(C_1 t)\sin(t)\), with sliders for constants \(C_1 = 1.1\) and \(C_2 = 1\). The “Show Parametric Curve” and “Show Tangent Vector” checkboxes are selected. The plotted curve forms a dense rose-petal pattern (spirograph-like), with many overlapping loops filling a roughly circular region of radius 2 centered at the origin. A green point marks the current position at parameter value \(s = 2\), located at approximately \((-0.67, 1.47)\), and a purple arrow shows the tangent vector at that point.

Page 12

Simple IVP 1 — Uncoupled System (Setup)

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2x \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 3y \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x \\ 3y \end{bmatrix}\]

Uncoupled means \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) only has \(x\) (no \(y\)), and \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\) only has \(y\) (no \(x\)). So we can use tools from the beginning of the term to solve each equation separately — both are separable.

Page 13

Simple IVP 1 — Solving the Uncoupled System

Starting with the \(x\)-equation and using separation of variables:

  1. \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2x\)
  2. \(\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{x}\,\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2\)
  3. \(\Rightarrow\quad \displaystyle\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \int 2\,dt\)
  4. \(\Rightarrow\quad \ln|x| = 2t + C_0\)
  5. \(\Rightarrow\quad x = C_1 e^{2t}\)

Similarly, solving the \(y\)-equation by the same method:

\[y = C_2 e^{3t}\]

Page 14

Simple IVP 1 — General and Particular Solution

From the previous page, the general solution is:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} C_1 e^{2t} \\ C_2 e^{3t} \end{bmatrix}\]

Applying the initial condition \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\):

\[\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} C_1 e^{0} \\ C_2 e^{0} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} C_1 \\ C_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\]

\(\Rightarrow\) Smooth Parametric Solution Curve (particular). The particular solution is:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} \\ 3e^{3t} \end{bmatrix}\]

Page 15

Simple IVP 1 — Phase Portrait Observations

Diagram description: A GeoGebra phase portrait is shown for the system \(f(x,y) = 2x\), \(g(x,y) = 3y\), so \(\mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2x \\ 3y \end{bmatrix}\). Parameters \(C_1 = 1\), \(C_2 = 3\), and the parametric solution curve \(r(t) = \text{Curve}((C_1 e^{2t},\, C_2 e^{3t}),\, t, \ldots)\) is drawn in red. The vector field shows arrows pointing outward from the origin in all four quadrants. Starting at \((1,3)\) (blue dot), the red trajectory curves steeply upward and slightly rightward, moving rapidly away from the origin along a path that hugs near the \(y\)-axis.

Observations:

  1. \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) is a source.
  2. Flow moves along the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes.
  3. Flow moves toward the \(y\)-axis and away from the \(x\)-axis.

Page 16

Simple IVP 1 — Activity

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -x \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 5y \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} -x \\ 5y \end{bmatrix}\]

By the same separation of variables approach:

General Solution:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} C_1 e^{-t} \\ C_2 e^{5t} \end{bmatrix}\]

Particular Solution (applying \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(C_1 = 2,\, C_2 = 2\)):

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 2e^{-t} \\ 2e^{5t} \end{bmatrix}\]

Page 17

Simple IVP 1 — Activity: Phase Portrait Observations

Diagram description: A GeoGebra phase portrait is shown for the system \(f(x,y) = -x\), \(g(x,y) = 5y\), so \(\mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} -x \\ 5y \end{bmatrix}\). Parameters \(C_1 = 2\), \(C_2 = 2\), and the parametric curve \(r(t) = \text{Curve}((C_1 e^{-t},\, C_2 e^{5t}),\, t, \ldots)\) is drawn. The vector field shows arrows pointing leftward (toward the \(y\)-axis) horizontally, and upward (away from the \(x\)-axis) vertically. Starting at \((2,2)\) (blue dot), the trajectory moves sharply upward as the \(y\)-component grows rapidly, while the \(x\)-component decays toward zero.

Observations:

  1. \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) is a saddle equilibrium.
  2. Flow moves along the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes.
  3. Flow moves toward the origin along the \(x\)-axis and away from the origin along the \(y\)-axis.

Page 18

Simple IVP 1 — Uncoupled System Overview

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 \\ y_0 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = by \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} ax \\ by \end{bmatrix}\]

General Solution:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} C_1 e^{at} \\ C_2 e^{bt} \end{bmatrix}\]

Particular Solution:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 e^{at} \\ y_0 e^{bt} \end{bmatrix}\]

Observations: The \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes are flow lines. \((0,0)\) is the equilibrium.

  • \(a, b > 0 \;\Rightarrow\) Source
  • \(a, b < 0 \;\Rightarrow\) Sink
  • Mixed signs \(\Rightarrow\) Saddle
